t: Number of Ways to Build House of Cards: Subset Counting
o: A house of cards is built bottom-up from n cards: a row of t triangles uses 2t leaning cards plus t - 1 horizontal cards between neighbors — exactly 3t - 1 cards. Every triangle on a row above the first must rest on a horizontal card below, and a row with t triangles offers only t - 1 such slots, so higher rows hold strictly fewer triangles; the leftmost-placement rule then makes each house a unique arrangement once its sequence of row sizes is fixed. For n = 16 exactly two houses exist (rows of 4 then 2 triangles, or 5 then 1); for n = 2 a single lone triangle uses both cards. Since sizes strictly decrease, a house is nothing but a subset of row types {2, 5, 8, 11, ...} whose costs sum to n, so counting houses becomes subset counting over at most about n/3 item types.
k: A row of t triangles consumes exactly 3t - 1 cards: two per triangle plus one horizontal between adjacent triangles.
Each higher row needs strictly fewer triangles because it must fit onto the t - 1 horizontal slots below, forcing strictly decreasing row sizes.
Strictly decreasing sizes mean order is forced, so counting houses equals counting subsets of weights {2, 5, 8, ...} summing to n — a classic 0/1 knapsack count.

a.i: Mirror the construction directly: go(left, cap) counts houses that spend exactly left more cards when every remaining row may hold at most cap triangles; the first call uses cap = n so the bottom row is unconstrained apart from its budget. Try every row size t whose 3t - 1 cards fit the budget and whose size respects the cap, recurse with the tightened bound t - 1, and add 1 whenever the budget lands exactly on zero. Memoization on (left, cap) keeps the state space small since budgets shrink by at least two cards per level.
s: Define go(left, cap): ways to build a tower of rows with sizes <= cap using exactly left cards.
For each t from 1 to min(cap, (left + 1) / 3) (so the row fits the budget), recurse on go(left - (3t - 1), t - 1).
a.t: O(n^2) — at most O(n) card budgets times O(n/3) caps, with bounded work per state.

a.n: Approach 2: One-Dimensional 0/1 Knapsack Over Row Types
a.i: Because strictly decreasing sizes fix the arrangement, a house corresponds to choosing each possible row size at most once. That is precisely 0/1 knapsack counting: process weights w = 3t - 1 for t = 1, 2, ... in any fixed order, and update dp[j] += dp[j - w] from high j down to w so each weight is used at most once per subset. dp[0] = 1 seeds the empty selection and dp[n] accumulates all valid houses.
s: Initialize dp[0] = 1 and all other dp[j] = 0.
Iterate weights w = 2, 5, 8, ... while w <= n.
For each weight, sweep j from n down to w and add dp[j - w] to dp[j].
a.t: O(n^2 / 3) — roughly n/3 weights each triggering an O(n) backward sweep.

w: The knapsack reformulation is the interview showpiece — realizing that "rows shrink strictly, so a house is just a set of row sizes" collapses a geometry problem into textbook subset counting; Approach 1 is the safer derivation if the reduction does not click immediately. Pitfalls: miscounting cards per row (it is 3t - 1, not 3t or 2t + 1), forgetting that equal-size rows are impossible, and sweeping the knapsack array forward instead of backward, which would allow reusing a row type. Edge cases: n = 1 returns 0 and n = 2 returns 1. Natural follow-ups include limiting the number of rows, or finding the minimum leftover cards when an exact build is impossible.
